title: Use an Example
summary: Here is the best secret every pro engineer knows: every good library comes with working example code!

steps.title: Use an Example

quickCheck.question: Where can you find pre-made starter sketches that show how to use an installed library?
options: Under File > Examples in the Arduino IDE menu
Under Edit > Cut in the top menu
quickCheck.explanation: The File > Examples menu lists built-in example sketches provided by installed libraries.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Libraries include working examples under File > Examples so you can test them immediately!

quickCheck.question: Why is testing an official example sketch a smart first step when trying new hardware?
options: It proves your wiring and library work before you write your own code
It deletes old sketches so you have more disk space
It makes the Arduino board waterproof
quickCheck.explanation: If an official example works, you know your hardware, wires, and library are good. If your custom code later fails, you know exactly where the bug is!
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Starting with known working code eliminates guesswork about whether the problem is in your wiring or your code.

steps.title: Anatomy of a Hardware Starter Sketch
Displaying Your First Message on Hardware
steps.markdownContent:
When you flash an example sketch to physical hardware, there's one physical trick that trips up almost every beginner!

You upload the code successfully, the backlight turns on, but... **no letters appear!** Is the code broken? Is the Arduino dead?

Nope! The LCD contrast potentiometer on the back of the backpack simply needs to be adjusted with a small screwdriver.

Interact with the contrast simulator below: adjust the potentiometer until `Monster Lab!` displays sharp, high-contrast characters on the screen!

interactiveConfig.title: LCD Contrast Tuning: Getting the Example to Show

steps.title: Knowledge Check: Working with Examples
steps.markdownContent: Test your understanding of opening, running, and verifying library example sketches.

interactiveConfig.question: What does LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2); tell the program?
options: Create an LCD object at I2C address 0x27 with 16 columns and 2 rows
Buy an LCD from website #27 for 16 dollars
interactiveConfig.explanation: The constructor parameters configure the I2C bus address (0x27) and screen dimensions (16 characters wide by 2 lines tall).

questions.question: What does LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2); tell the program?
options: Create an LCD object at I2C address 0x27 with 16 columns and 2 rows
Buy an LCD from website #27 for 16 dollars
questions.explanation: The constructor parameters configure the I2C bus address (0x27) and screen dimensions (16 characters wide by 2 lines tall).

questions.question: Why does the example sketch include <Wire.h> alongside <LiquidCrystal_I2C.h>?
options: Wire.h handles the low-level I2C hardware bus communication used by the LCD backpack
Wire.h is required to supply electricity to the computer mouse
Wire.h turns the Arduino into a speaker
questions.explanation: Wire.h is Arduino's standard I2C library; LiquidCrystal_I2C depends on Wire.h to send electrical packets.

questions.question: If your example sketch compiles and uploads with zero errors but the screen shows only solid blank rectangles, what should you inspect first?
options: Adjust the blue contrast potentiometer on the back of the LCD backpack
Smash the Arduino with a hammer
questions.explanation: Solid rectangles or completely blank screens almost always mean the contrast trimmer potentiometer needs tuning.
